reason: The standard names the danger zone as Level I food safety in words; the clause carries the cooling law too, but its heading is the danger zone and ties break down.
The standard names cross-contamination as Level I food safety: storage order, colour-coded boards, hands and towels as vectors.
The standard names FIFO as Level I food safety; the clause mentions HACCP and the allergen protocol in passing, but its heading is FIFO and ties break down.
The standard names inspections as Level III food safety: the jurisdiction's system, the visit and the crisis playbooks.
The closing principle of the inspections entry (crises inevitable, scandals optional, the binder) belongs with inspections, which the standard places at Level III.
The standard names the two-hour rule as Level I food safety in words.
The guide states shallow pans and ice baths inside the cooling law's own sentence, and the standard names the cooling law as Level II food safety with no separate line for its method.
The standard names HACCP as a system (identify, control, document) as Level II food safety.
The standard names the allergen protocol as Level II food safety.
A line of the FIFO clause about the everyday disciplines being the licence for the rest; it sits with FIFO at Level I and ties break down.
The standard names the jurisdiction framing (letter grades, point scores, risk-based frequency) as Level IV food safety.
Running the kitchen so any moment is inspection-ready is the inspections entry's central claim, and the standard places inspections at Level III.
The standard names the disciplines at Level III in words, and this fact is the guide's own list of the disciplines (temps logged, FIFO labelled, hand sinks used, sanitiser titrated).
